{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"An online age-checking system can become identity infrastructure long before anyone admits that identity is the project. Legislators may call it a “narrow safety measure,” and vendors may describe a quick gate that merely sorts adults from children. But the gate has to recognize something about you, remember enough to trust the result, and communicate that trust to someone else. I think that's the hinge: safety at the front door – identity in the walls.

Start with the question: what must you prove before a site lets you through? A system might inspect a document, estimate age from a face, consult an account, or ask another service to vouch for you. Those methods differ, of course (and their risks differ), but every reusable result needs a handle: this person was checked, this result is current, this gatekeeper accepts it. The handle may be called a token rather than an identity. That doesn't make it harmless.

Once you've got a handle, pressure builds to reuse it. A game wants your age today; a forum wants it tomorrow; a shop wants confidence next week. Rechecking from scratch costs time and money, so the attractive engineering answer is a credential (a tidy word for a durable fact about a person). The credential becomes portable, the verifier becomes central, and a temporary question hardens into a standing relationship. The system isn't checking age anymore – it's deciding which version of you other services are allowed to believe.

This is where the sales pitch turns into bullshit. If you buy a ticket and the clerk glances at proof of age, the glance ends. Online, you're offered the digital equivalent of that glance, but the machinery may require identifiers, logs, issuers, rules for revocation, and a way to resolve errors. Together they form a control panel for your participation (usually operated by somebody you didn't choose). A narrow gate has become a checkpoint network, piece by piece.

I don't need to claim a conspiracy to see the danger. Incentives can do the work. A service that answers “is this user old enough?” can be asked whether the user is local, licensed, sanctioned, employable, or entitled to speak. Some may even be legitimate in a bounded setting. To me, the governing issue is who can add questions, who can link answers, and whether we can refuse the expansion. Our danger comes from function creep with paperwork.

Parents are easy to corner here. You care about your child's safety, so opponents of the system can be painted as indifferent to harm. But care isn't consent to build a lifelong credential. The practical test is simple: can your child leave the system behind, or does one childhood check become the seed of an adult identity record? If the answer depends on a vendor's promise, you've received a policy assurance – it isn't a structural limit. Promises travel badly when ownership, law, or panic changes.

I'd ask four things of any proposal: what information enters, what leaves, who can demand another use, and how a person recovers after an error. Then ask whether the design prevents linkage (rather than merely discouraging it), whether records expire, and whether access remains possible when the checker fails. We should demand architecture that makes abuse difficult, because policy language alone can't keep a narrow tool narrow. That is the difference between an age check and an identity regime.

We can protect children without pretending that infrastructure has only its first advertised purpose. A machine built to recognize, remember, and authorize people is an identity machine, whatever label sits on the box. The question for privacy advocates and parents is larger than whether one check seems tolerable today. It is whether our children, and the rest of us, will have to carry that check from door to door. Keep the glance; reject the checkpoint. That choice belongs to all of us, before the concrete sets.","omitted":[],"refused":""}
